content: Ferrite, also known as alpha iron (α-Fe), refers to a specific form of iron or a solid solution where iron is the primary constituent. It possesses a body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. This structure is responsible for the magnetic properties observed in steel and cast iron, making ferrite a quintessential example of a ferromagnetic material. Essentially, ferrite can be regarded as nearly pure iron, with a tensile strength of approximately 280 N/mm². Ferrite is strictly defined as a solid solution of iron in the BCC phase, containing a maximum of 0.03% carbon at 723°C and only 0.006% carbon at room temperature. In most mild steels, which are plain carbon steels with up to about 0.2 weight percent carbon, ferrite constitutes the majority of the microstructure. As the carbon content increases, the proportion of pearlite—a fine lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite—also increases. Since both bainite and pearlite contain ferrite as a component, any iron-carbon alloy will inherently include some amount of ferrite if it is allowed to reach equilibrium at room temperature. In pure iron, ferrite remains stable at temperatures below 910°C. When the temperature exceeds 910°C, the crystal structure transitions to a face-centered cubic (FCC) form known as austenite (γ-iron). At even higher temperatures, above 1390°C and up to the melting point of 1539°C, the BCC structure reappears in the form of delta ferrite (δ-Fe), which is the stable phase in this temperature range. The solubility of carbon in ferrite is extremely limited, with a maximum of approximately 0.02 weight percent at 723°C. This limited solubility arises because carbon atoms dissolve interstitially in the iron lattice. However, the carbon atoms are significantly larger than the interstitial spaces in the BCC structure, being roughly twice the diameter of these holes. As a result, each carbon atom creates a strong local strain field in the surrounding lattice. This leads to a positive enthalpy of mixing, which is thermodynamically unfavorable. Nevertheless, the entropy contribution to the free energy of solution stabilizes the structure at low carbon concentrations. At 723°C, a critical temperature in the iron-carbon system, a eutectoid reaction occurs. At this temperature, austenite (with 0.8 weight percent carbon) decomposes into a mixture of ferrite and cementite. This reaction marks the minimum temperature at which austenite is stable in the iron-carbon phase diagram.
